name: Victor Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything here is confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computing and a bit of Year 7 science at Brookfield Academy, a small secondary in a commuter town where most parents work in the city. I'm in at quarter to eight, check the computer suite hasn't been sabotaged, then teach four or five lessons, mostly Python basics and spreadsheets. I use AI tools every day, for planning, for writing example code, for checking the kids' projects. Two evenings a week I tutor online through an app to make the rent work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being the only computing teacher, so there's nobody to ask, and I'm still learning how to run a room. My line manager, Mr Bryce, is a physics teacher who says my lessons are fun but chaotic. I rent a room in a shared house on Station Road and have maybe two weeks of money in the bank, so the tutoring isn't optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on the staff chat that it's a shame, because the tools were genuinely useful, but fine, the basics still matter. Online I'd probably post a slightly smug thread about which tools were worth it and which were rubbish. With friends I'd shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's okay for me, my job and the subject carry on. The money's still tight, though, because I'm on the bottom of the pay scale with a room rent that went up twelve percent this year. AI fizzling doesn't fix my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I already use for planning and code examples, because they still save me time. I'd add a third tutoring evening to build a buffer. And I'd ask Mr Bryce for help with the chaos, maybe watching a calmer colleague teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, slightly restless. I'd be a bit bored, honestly. And still checking my balance before buying lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tutoring isn't optional. How much does it bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and fifty a month. The tutoring app pays me nine pounds for a half-hour lesson, and that money is the difference between a normal month and an overdraft month. I don't love giving up my evenings, but it's that or a second job in a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stalls, does your computing subject feel safer or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, mostly. Schools still need someone to teach coding and spreadsheets, and there aren't many computing teachers around here. Brookfield struggled to fill my post before me, so I'm not easy to replace.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, as the tools were useful, but the basics still matter.
I'd post a thread online about **which tools** were worth it and which were rubbish.
think: I think my **job and subject** carry on unchanged.
I think money stays tight on the bottom of the **pay scale** with rising rent.
do: Keep using **AI tools** for planning and code examples.
Add a **third tutoring evening** to build a buffer.
Ask Mr Bryce to let him **watch a calmer colleague** teach.
feel: He feels **mostly fine**, slightly restless and a little bored.
He still **checks his balance** before buying lunch.
S0.quote: The tutoring app pays me nine pounds for a half-hour lesson, and that money is the difference between a normal month and an overdraft month.
fieldNote: He sees his post as **hard to replace**, as computing teachers are scarce locally.
His real pressure is **thin money**: a rent rise and evening tutoring he can't drop.
He'd be **bored** by a plateau, which says a lot about his appetite for change.

steps.text: Keep using AI tools to plan lessons and write code examples
Add a third evening of online tutoring each week
Watch a calmer colleague teach to fix his classroom routines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools should teach kids to work with AI, not pretend it isn't there, and I'd offer to run training for staff. Online I'd share what's working in my classroom. With friends I'd say it's an exciting time, which is mostly true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's strange. I teach kids to code, and coding is the first thing on the list. I'm teaching a subject that's eating itself. If kids can ask a tool to write their program, I have to work out what I'm actually teaching them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first term I'd rewrite the Year 9 course around building things with AI, testing them and spotting where they go wrong. I'd ask the head to make me the school's digital lead, even for a small allowance. And I'd look for a second income that isn't tutoring, maybe marking coursework for the exam board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit dizzy. I like change, but I'm also the one standing on the bit that's moving. Some nights I think I've got the best job for this, and some nights the worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Coding is on the card. How does that sit with teaching computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Computing turns into teaching kids to think clearly, check answers and know when the machine's wrong. That's a real subject, but schools might decide it's something every teacher does, not a separate post. Then Brookfield doesn't need me as a computing teacher, it needs me as something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the tutoring app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that would go first. If parents can get an AI tutor for a tenner a month, nobody pays me nine pounds a lesson. I'd probably lose most of it within a year, which is a hundred and fifty a month I don't have.

say: I'd say schools should **teach kids** to work with AI, not ignore it.
I'd offer to run **staff training** and share what works in my classroom.
think: I think computing is a **subject eating itself**, as coding is first on the list.
I think my **tutoring income** disappears within a year to cheap AI tutors.
do: Rewrite the **Year 9 course** around building and checking things with AI.
Ask the head to make him the school's **digital lead**.
Look for **exam board marking** as a second income instead of tutoring.
feel: He feels **excited and dizzy**, standing on the bit that's moving.
S1.quote: I teach kids to code, and coding is the first thing on the list. I'm teaching a subject that's eating itself.
fieldNote: He spots the irony quickly: his **subject** is the one AI does first.
His side income from **tutoring** is the first money he expects to lose.
Adaptive and keen, he still feels **financially exposed** on a thin cushion.

steps.text: Rewrite the Year 9 computing course around building and testing with AI
Ask the head for the school digital lead role and allowance
Apply to mark coursework for the exam board

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a national plan for schools, quickly, because kids will be growing up with something smarter than their teachers. At work I'd volunteer to lead on it. Online I'd be calm and practical, posting guides rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job changes completely. My computing post probably goes in the first wave. Whoever knows the AI best and gets on with the kids might be the one they keep. I'd bet on being that person, but it's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd go to the head and pitch a role: AI lead across the academy trust, training staff and checking tools. I'd stop the tutoring before it dries up and put those evenings into a teaching qualification in maths, since maths teachers are always short. And I'd move out of the shared house into my brother's spare room to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. I'd feel like I'm running a race I might actually win. Then I'd remember I've got two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots for hands-on work about three years later. How much of your job is thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it is thinking work, so planning, coding, marking, explaining all change in 2028. The hands-on side is running a room of thirteen-year-olds, fixing the printers and standing at the gate, and robots for that wouldn't come till around 2031. So I'd have about three years where the job is mostly being a person in a room who understands the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Arjun, who's an electrician and earns more than me. He's said before I can use his spare room. I'd also talk to the bank about moving my overdraft limit, though I'd rather not need it.

I'd volunteer to lead and post **practical guides** online rather than panic.
think: I think my **computing post** probably goes in the first wave.
I think the school may keep whoever knows **AI best** and gets on with kids.

His **two weeks** of savings keep pulling him back down.
S2.quote: My computing post probably goes in the first wave. Whoever knows the AI best and gets on with the kids might be the one they keep.
fieldNote: He expects his **computing post** to go but bets on being kept in a new role.
He reads the **robot gap** as three years of being the person in the room.
His safety net is **family**: his brother Arjun's spare room.

steps.text: Pitch an AI lead role across the academy trust
Start a maths teaching qualification in his tutoring evenings
Give up the room on Station Road
Move into his brother Arjun's spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, so schools should start training everyone now. I'd be loud about it at work, in a friendly way. Online I'd keep posting what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is about right for me. I'd have time to get properly good at teaching, add maths, and become the AI person for the trust before 2031. By the time robots arrive around 2034, I'd want to be in a role that's about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the maths add-on qualification, paid by the trust if I can convince Mr Bryce. I'd build a staff training session on AI for planning and run it every half term. And I'd save fifty a month from the tutoring while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, honestly. With five years I can choose my exit instead of being pushed through it. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast picture I'd be grabbing whatever role was going. Here I can pick: maths and computing, or the trust's AI lead, or even moving towards training teachers. The extra three years turns panic into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Brookfield you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Doran in the office, who does all the timetabling and admissions. A tool would do that in an afternoon. And Mr Bryce, actually, because physics explanations are exactly what the AI is good at.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** for training everyone now.
I'd keep posting **what works** and be loud about it at work.
think: I think five years is **about right** for me to get good and add maths.
I think by 2034 I want a role **about people**.
do: Start the **maths add-on** qualification, ideally trust-funded.
Run a **staff training** session on AI planning every half term.
Save **fifty a month** from tutoring while it lasts.
feel: He feels **quite good**, able to choose rather than be pushed.
S3.quote: With five years I can choose my exit instead of being pushed through it.
fieldNote: Five years turns his **adaptability** into real choices: maths, AI lead or teacher training.
He worries for **office staff** and physics colleagues more than himself.
Thin savings keep him **uneasy**, but he has a workable plan.

steps.text: Start the maths add-on teaching qualification this year
Run a half-termly staff session on AI lesson planning
Save fifty a month from tutoring income while it lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we start now, and I'd want every school to have someone leading on it. With friends I'd say it's the most interesting time to be a teacher. Online I'd be the cheerful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me. Ten years is enough time to be the person who shows everyone else how it works. I'd be thirty-seven, experienced, and hopefully past the chaotic-lessons stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using AI every day, sharing what works. Over the next two years I'd add maths, and later maybe a master's in education technology, part-time. And I'd try to save a little, though honestly thin savings is the bit I'm worst at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, with the money nag. The job side feels good. The bank side never does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably leading digital learning across a few schools, still teaching some lessons because I'd miss the kids. Maybe training new teachers. Hopefully renting a flat on my own by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're in the middle politically. What should government do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund teachers to retrain properly, part-time and paid, instead of each school doing its own thing. Make sure the tools sold to schools are checked by someone independent. I don't need a big programme, just sensible rules and some money for training.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if every school has someone leading on it.
I'd tell friends it's the **most interesting time** to be a teacher.
think: I think a decade **suits me**, as I'd be experienced by thirty-seven.
I think I could be the person who **shows everyone else** how it works.
do: Keep **using AI daily** and sharing what works with colleagues.
Add **maths** within two years and maybe a part-time master's later.
Try to **save a little**, his weakest habit.
feel: He feels **calm-ish** about the job but never easy about the bank.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to be the person who shows everyone else how it works.
fieldNote: He sees the long warning as an **opportunity** to lead across schools.
His only real drag is **thin savings**, which he admits he's bad at building.
Centre politics shows in his ask: **sensible rules** and training money, not a big programme.

steps.text: Use AI daily in computing lessons and share methods with colleagues
Add a maths teaching qualification within two years
Set up a standing order into savings each payday

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be betting everything on being the one they keep, with two weeks of money. What would help is paid, part-time retraining for teachers and someone checking the tools schools buy. Every school will need one teacher who understands the machines and still likes kids more than machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the kids think. My Year 10s already ask why they should learn to code if the AI does it. I don't have a great answer yet, and I'd like one before 2028.

headlineQuote: Every school will need one teacher who understands the machines and still likes kids more than machines.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old **computing teacher**, the only one at a small commuter-town academy.
He uses **AI every day** and tutors online two evenings a week to cover rent.
He has about **two weeks** of savings and leans on his brother as a safety net.
He's most worried in the fast pictures because his **own subject** is what AI does first.
With more warning he sees himself **leading digital learning** across schools.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, betting on being **the one kept** with two weeks of money.
whatWouldHelp: Paid, **part-time retraining** for teachers and independent checks on school AI tools.
